The Nādakārikā composed by Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha,
together with the commentary composed by Aghoraśivācārya.

A sound distinct from intellect, ego, mind, knowledge, attachment, and limited agency (kalā), as well as from Māyā, the individual soul, and power (śakti), is perceived even beyond [ordinary] sounds. || 1 ||
Having bowed to Śiva, who transcends sound (nāda), for the sake of establishing the knowledge of sound,
I shall explain the *Nādakārikā* composed by the venerable Rāmakaṇṭha.

*Asmitā* is the sense of "I-ness" (*ahaṅkāra*). Consequently, since the principles beginning with *buddhi* and ending with *māyā* are established by their own respective effects alone, and there is no evidence for their being causes of any other effects, and because the *puruṣa* and its power are immutable, it is impossible for speech to be inherent in them; furthermore, gross sounds are subject to production and destruction.

Because [the manifestation] depends on other causes, and because by the word "also" (api) it is indicated that the phonemes produced from that [manifestation] cannot function as denoters due to their sequential occurrence, the *nāda* is seen as their cause; the meaning is that it is ascertained by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). || 1 ||
For instance:
Phonemes, which are perceivable by the auditory organ, perish as soon as they are uttered and exist in a temporal sequence;
since they cannot assist one another, they are not logically capable of being denoters of meaning in an undifferentiated state. (2)

Now, one might object: let it be that words themselves, through the division into base and suffix, are the causes for the cognition of meaning; or let it be that the sentence itself—characterized by the connection between a specific action and its factors—is the cause of that [cognition]. To this, he says:
"Nor is any word heard as distinct from the phonemes, nor any sentence."

Since it has been stated that phonemes— which constitute parts of words and sentences— lack mutual assistance due to their momentary destruction, and since words and sentences distinct from those [phonemes] are not perceived separately,
they too cannot be denotative; thus, because their existence is refuted by perception, he states that their existence is not established even by inference:
That which was previously negated as "not a sense-object" (akṣa) is now negated as "existent" (sat) in order for it to be known through other means.
He elaborates on this very point by first raising an objection: "If the word 'cow'—consisting of name and so forth—is perceived by the ear and thus exists as a reality, it is not so."
For there is nothing else here apart from the letter *ga*, the vowel *au*, and the visarga.
By the inclusion of "etcetera" in the phrase "name, etcetera," qualifying words such as "red" and so forth, as well as verbal expressions such as "goes" and so forth, are included.
And therefore:
because they do not exist simultaneously, the prior two do not exist at the time of perceiving the other;
thus, from the *visarjanīya* that has already occurred, there is no manifestation of consciousness characterized by *khura* and *kambala*. (5)

The manifestation of consciousness is the arising of the cognition of an object. The point is that if [the suffix] were produced from the visarga alone, then even in cases such as "aśvaḥ" (horse) and "puruṣaḥ" (person), there would be the cognition of a dewlap and so forth. || 5 ||

One might object: "Granted that the cognition of meaning does not arise from the *visarjanīya* alone; however, it certainly arises when [the *visarjanīya*] is conjoined with the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the preceding phonemes.
For even though phonemes perish in an instant, their impressions are not destroyed, since we observe their recollection at a later time. Thus he raises this doubt:

Now, if it is argued that the cognition of the meaning is indeed desired [to arise] from the visarga when assisted by the phonetic refinement (*saṃskṛti*) produced by the preceding vowel, provided that such a cognition does not occur from the visarga alone; (6)

He refutes this: "This is not so; for even those formative factors (*saṃskāra*) by which [impressions] were previously deposited in the intellect would not be causes of consciousness, such that a cognition of an object could thereby be postulated. (7)

For it is observed that mental formations (*saṃskāra*) serve as the causes of memory only for those objects, such as jars and the like, which have been previously experienced and projected into the mind, and not for unexperienced objects such as jars. Therefore, in this case as well, it is logical that those phonemes by which [the object] was deposited in the mind are themselves the causes of cognition, and not the meaning of the word or the sentence.

The capacity to convey meaning is not possible [in that case]. As they have said: "Indeed, when mental impressions (*saṃskāras*) are manifested by the appearance of the form of a certain object and serve as the cause for cognition, then no cognition of that object is postulated from those [impressions].
If it is argued that a word (*pada*), consisting of a collection of phonemes (*varṇa*) both being remembered and being experienced, is the signifier, that is not so.
Because it is not observed that lamps which are being remembered possess the capacity to illuminate objects;

and because, as has been stated, it is impossible for phonemes to convey meaning, it follows by the principle of "otherwise inexplicability" (anyathānupapatti) that there must exist something else entirely distinct from them— which is manifested by them, inseparable [from them], and which, like the fluid within a peacock's egg, manifests many phonemes in a sequential order.

The Grammarians maintain that the *sphoṭa*—which is both identical to and distinct from the phonemes (*pada*), whose nature is that of the sentence (*vākya*), which is all-pervading and eternal because it is the cause of the simultaneous or successive comprehension of meaning for the entire world, and which alone makes the meaning manifest to those engaged in linguistic usage—must be accepted. However, this is not tenable; for instance: therein...

As for what was stated—that the *sphoṭa* is distinct from the phonemes—that is incorrect. It is not tenable for that *sphoṭa* to exist between the phonemes and the means of its apprehension as something separate from the phonemes. For is it distinct from the phonemes or non-distinct?
First, it cannot be distinct, because, being distinct from the phonemes, it is not perceived despite meeting the conditions for perception, just like a rabbit's horn or similar things.

Nor is its existence established through inference, because that [inference] is sublated by perception. Nor should it be said that its being accessible to perception is unestablished, because it is a cognizer (*jñāpaka*). For a causal factor, such as the sense organs, produces an effect even when unknown through its very capacity, just like seeds and the like which possess latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). This is unlike a cognizer, such as the winking of an eye.

Since its status as an indicator is impossible, there is no infinite regress resulting from inference. Furthermore, the sphoṭa must not be accepted as a non-indicator, because—like a wink of the eye—it does not indicate a relationship beforehand; thus, how can it be conceptualized as something unperceived like the sense organs? When it is non-different [from the phonemes], then the phoneme itself is the sphoṭa, and it does not exist as something distinct from them.

Just as "hasta" and "kara" are synonymous, so too are "sphoṭa" and "varṇa" identical in their usage, because they denote the same object; therefore, there is no difference in meaning here due to a difference in those terms. By means of that [sphoṭa], the cognition of the meaning is logically established. As for what was also said—that [the sphoṭa] is manifested by the phonemes (varṇas)—that too is incorrect, because the sphoṭa...
Indeed, is the cause for the cognition of the meaning manifested by many phonemes collectively, or by each one individually?

If it were manifested by many, then—since those [phonemes] perish as soon as they are uttered—the *ga* and *au* would not exist at the time of the *visarjanīya*; thus, the manifestation of that [meaning] from the *visarjanīya* alone would not occur, and the previously mentioned defect remains. Now, if [it is argued that] the final [phoneme], accompanied by the preceding impressions (*saṃskāra*)...

If it is claimed that the phoneme (*varṇa*) is what manifests that [sphoṭa], then the same fault applies there as well; for what reason, then, is the absolutely unestablished *sphoṭa* postulated? Now, regarding the second [position]: since many *sphoṭas*—such as those of "cow," "gavaya," and "sky"—would be manifested by the letter *ga*, there would be no distinction between them, resulting in the undesirable consequence of the cognition of multiple meanings simultaneously. Furthermore, if [the sphoṭa] were all-pervading (*vibhu*),...

Furthermore, since there would be no distinction [in the word] when it is manifested by the phonemes uttered by a single person, there would be a comprehension of meaning for cognizers even in another location; likewise, it would occur at another time as well, because, being eternal, there is no difference in what is imparted to it. Yet such is not the case. Therefore, it is not logical that anything—whether all-pervading (*vibhu*) or eternal—could be a communicator of meaning, let alone the *sphoṭa*.

He states the opponent's intention in another way: "If it is argued that the cognition of a sequence [of phonemes] occurring in succession is the basis for the mental apprehension of that [word], and is thus accepted as the faultless denoter of the class of gross words, then [we reply:]... (8)

For it is evident that, having first determined through the intellect an object characterized by its hooves, dewlap, and so forth, and having mentally associated with it the corresponding word "cow" and the like, one then employs the gross term [“sthūla”]. Subsequently, this [term]—
supported by the word "cow" and so forth which has been mounted upon the intellect, and accompanied by the sequence of intended objects such as the cow and the gavaya— is [employed].

Alternatively, let it be accepted that consciousness itself—arising in the form of each respective object, serving as the cause for the utterance of each corresponding gross sound, and consisting of the very activity of the intellect—is the faultless designator of objects such as "cow" and so forth, occurring in succession. (8)
This too he refutes:
"Let it be that the denotative power is not distinct from the denoted objects;
therefore, that entity would be apprehended by the intellect in its entirety and without any distinction whatsoever. (9)
In this way, let there be denotative power belonging to the internal reflective awareness (*parāmarśajñāna*). This being so, there is non-difference between the signified and the signifier;

for both possess the nature of the dewlap and so forth, since they share a single cause, and because that object consisting of the dewlap and so forth is, without exception, mounted upon the intellect by means of its specific external form. || 9 ||
Here, an objection regarding a distinction is raised:

"If it is argued that the very nature of being the signifier (*vācaka*) is the distinction from the signified (*vācya*), because [the signifier] consists of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of that [signified]; yet this [reflective awareness] has the signified as its object of reflection, whether through difference or non-difference, and this [signified] exists. (10)

This alone is the distinction of this mental form (*buddhyākāra*), which is the signifier (*vācaka*), from the external form which is the signified (*vācya*): namely, that its status as a signifier consists in its being of the nature of a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the external form. Consequently, the various external forms characterized as "cow" and so forth become the signified when they are being reflected upon by the various cognitions of reflective awareness that serve as signifiers.
This is the distinction. To this it is replied: "And this [is] existent, but how so? (10)

That sound which consists of internal discourse, by which objects such as form, taste, smell, and sound are brought to the state of being perceived— that sound is established not as an object of the senses.
It is indeed true that there exists this internal consciousness, which is distinct from the object of speech and consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

However, it does not arise without a cause, because it is occasional (*kādācitkatva*). This is what is meant: for cognition is observed to determine an object only when that object has been made an objective domain by the external senses, such as the eye, and not when it has not been so made an objective domain, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, [this] internal cognition...

One performs reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) only toward an object that has been made an object of cognition by someone; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of reflecting upon all objects at all times.
Therefore, that very thing by which objects such as form, taste, and so forth are brought to the state of being reflected upon by the speaker’s intellect is here called *nāda*.
"Consisting of internal discourse" (*antaḥ-saṃjalpātman*): that of which internal discourse, whose nature is the form of the *bindu*, exists as its effect.

It is of such a kind: even for that reflective cognition (*parāmarśajñāna*), the cause is established as being the expressive word (*vācaka*), and not as a gross sound (*sthūlaśabda*) transformed into the form of the object. If it is asked, "How then does the sound residing in the speaker produce the cognition of the denoted object in the hearer? [the answer is: it is the sound produced by that [speaker], manifested by the gross word uttered, which resides in the hearer.
He will state in the conclusion of the kārikā that sound also produces the cognition of the object to be expressed. || 11 ||
This alone is the denotative word that takes all words and their meanings as its objects, and no other;
for that which is seen as existent is thereby always apprehended as non-existent.

As it has been said: "There is no cognition in the world that is not accompanied by words; here, every knowledge arises as permeated by speech" (*Vākyapadīya* 1.115). But how, then, is it stated in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*: "The final phoneme, joined with the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the preceding phonemes, is the signifier"?
There is no fault, because it is a figurative designation based on its manifesting the sound (nāda). || 12 ||
Having thus established that sound (nāda) possesses the capacity to signify meaning, he states the previously asserted fact that intellect (buddhi) and the others are its causes:
"The form of the intellect does not arise from us, nor is it the product of mind or ego."
Thus, the unmanifest is distinct from the transformations of its effects—the body and the senses. || 13 ||

It has been stated that this quality of being a designator (vācakatva) does not belong to the form of the intellect (buddhyākāra) for the very reason already mentioned. Nor is it distinct from the mind (manas) and the ego (ahaṅkāra). Similarly, the unmanifest (avyakta) is also not intended as a designator; this is the remainder [of the argument], because it is established solely as the cause of the qualities (guṇas), and there is a lack of evidence for its being the cause of any other effect. || 13 ||

And this [sound], because it is unmanifest, is the subtle *nāda*; however, as sound (*śabda*), it is differentiated into sentences and words by virtue of its denotative function, since it is from this that there arises the non-confusion of the cognition of word-meanings. (14)

Since the non-confusion of the cognition of word-meanings is observed among cognizers, therefore, in each person, this sound—which exists as the denoter within those sentences and words—is of a distinct form; it is designated as "unmanifest" (avyakta) due to its subtlety, and as "gross" (sthūla) due to its quality as a denoter. || 14 ||

Having thus described the nature of Nāda, he speaks in order to establish Mahāmāyā as its cause: "And yet, it is not perceived in that same way by the multitudes of fettered beings (paśu), such as cowherds and women; therefore, sounds are divided by the ignorant (bāla) and are associated with birth and dissolution. (15)

For here, at the time of a single person’s reflection, since the arising of all [sounds] is not observed, distinct sounds are experienced according to the differences in their respective states, caused by individual selves (*paśvātman*) whose natures are mutually different;
these are also perceived through scripture and because the cognition of word-meanings would otherwise be inexplicable.

As it has been said: "From cowherds and women to children, from barbarians to those who speak common tongues, even the beings dwelling within the water—they too always speak thus. What follows from this? To this he says: "Regarding origination and cessation" (*utpattyapavarga*). By that reason, their nature of having the characteristics of origination and destruction—that is, their being effects—is established; such is the meaning. || 15 ||
Therefore, their material cause must be stated as that which is to be produced;
thus established is the Supreme Nāda, Sumaṅgalā, Mālinī, and Mahāmāyā.
The unstruck bindu, the soundless speech, the Brahma-kuṇḍalinī—this is called the principle (tattva) known as Vidyā; thus it has been stated in various scriptures by those [teachers]. (17)
Having restated the opponent's intention, he refutes it:
"This state [of speech] is described by some experts in words as belonging to the power of action (*kriyāśakti*);
however, in this system, something else is stated, namely that speech does not inhere in the person (*puruṣa*). (18)

Since it is not logical for sound to be produced by a sequence beginning with *nāda* due to the absence of an inherent connection (*samavāya*) between each individual person and speech—because that would entail the consequence of [the self] being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*)—this [theory] has certainly not been stated here. 18.

He elaborates on this very point: "The Self is said here to be unchangeable, and its power likewise; therefore, those two are not capable of existing in many ways, because, being devoid of consciousness, they would be subject to modification. (19)
That Kuṇḍalinī is distinct from that male power (puṃśakti) by virtue of being the material cause of Nāda;
therefore, it is established that Kuṇḍalinī, distinct from each individual soul and its power, is the cause of Nāda. || 19 ||
If this is so, one might think that Māyā alone is the transformative (pariṇāminī) cause and not the material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa); therefore, he says:
"Even though it is non-conscious (acid), because of its purity, it is distinct from Māyā and is said to be situated above it. (20)
As it has been said: "Above Māyā is Mahāmāyā" (Raurava Saṃhitā 4.28). || 20 ||
And he says that this Mahāmāyā, which is established by the authority of scripture and serves as the material cause for the pure path (śuddhādhvan), is as follows:

"The pure principle of Vidyā and the world-realm that bestows enjoyment upon the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) are taught in the sacred scriptures (sadāgama) along with other paths; and she is the cause for that [liberation], which leads to the highest good. (21)
One who is proficient in the Brahman that is speech attains the Brahman that is consciousness, as they say:
"He who is proficient in the Brahman that is sound attains the supreme Brahman" (Maitrī Upaniṣad 6.22).
Furthermore—
Success, liberation, and the supreme [state], as well as the knowledge and action of Nāda, become fruitful. || 22 ||
"They speak"—this connects back to the previously mentioned action. || 22 ||

If this is so, since supreme liberation is established through the knowledge of the Sound (*nāda*) alone, why is it stated in the venerable *Svāyaṃbhuva* and other scriptures that initiation alone is the liberator? We shall explain that even knowledge is a means to liberation only as a subsidiary element of initiation, and not by itself. Furthermore, regarding the gross sound belonging to Māyā, which takes the form of a fetter—

Since it is impossible for [the Veda] to establish pure entities such as Śiva and so forth, he states— by way of its being the cause of pure sound in the form of mantra and tantra— that this [purity] is established:
"because of being the cause of mantra and so forth."

Therefore, it is stated in the venerable *Mataṅga* and other scriptures that within these sounds, which are like glowing coals, there exist subtle mantra-sounds, which are like fire, that become effective when manifested. Consequently, this aforementioned *nāda*, which is the effect of those [subtle sounds], is as follows:
It is distinct from the sheaths of ignorance, passion, and the rest;
it is distinct from their effects, because of [the soul's] lack of attachment and because of the union of vision and action. || 23 ||

Since passion (rāga), knowledge (vidyā), and limited agency (kalā) are established by their own respective effects alone, there is no evidence for their being causes of other effects; furthermore, it would entail the undesirable consequence of postulating numerous additional principles (tattvas). || 23 ||
That sound born of the Great Māyā is rightly the designator of the ultimate reality (paramārtha), by which the gross sound—the mantra consisting of the tantra—is set in motion. || 24 ||
But it has been stated that the gross [form] possesses denotative power because it manifests that [subtle form]. || 24 ||
Concluding this very point, he says:

"Since that expressive power of speech, which exists as the capacity for verbal expression, is distinct for each individual, it therefore creates the collection of signifiers within and then manifests them externally as well. (25)
Manifested through gross sounds, these subtle resonances consist of sound;
producing a cognition distinct from the denoted object, they increase the course of worldly existence.
And it has been stated that, by this very sequence, mantras—even as mere sounds—become the designators of objects such as Śiva;
thus, the illustrious Bhaṭṭarāmakaṇṭha, the son of Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha, composed this *Nādasiddhi* here in twenty-five verses in the Kāśmīra region. (27)
The *Nādasiddhi* has been explained by the illustrious Ghorāśivācārya, known by another name, at the request of the most excellent gurus.
